lead: This unit explains how multiple processes cooperate without corrupting data and how they avoid or recover from deadlocks. After studying it, you will be able to design safe critical sections, use locks, semaphores and monitors, and choose a correct dead‑lock handling technique for a given system.
about: Unit 3 has eight chapters that build step by step. Chapter 3.1 defines the critical‑section problem and race conditions. Chapter 3.2 shows Peterson’s software solution and the hardware primitives that support it. Chapter 3.3 introduces mutex locks and counting semaphores. Chapter 3.4 adds monitors with condition variables. Chapter 3.5 models deadlocks and lists the four necessary conditions. Chapter 3.6 covers prevention techniques. Chapter 3.7 (advanced) presents avoidance and the banker’s algorithm. Chapter 3.8 finishes with detection and recovery methods. Each chapter expands on the previous one, moving from basic mutual exclusion to full dead‑lock management.

chapters.idea: Identify race conditions and formulate the critical‑section problem.
chapters.depth: Define process, shared variable, and interleaving of instructions. Explain why two processes that read‑modify‑write the same variable can produce wrong results. List the three requirements of a correct solution: mutual exclusion, progress, and bounded waiting. Mention that some syllabi call this the "Critical‑Section Problem".

figure.title: Race condition
figure.aria: Shows two processes entering the same critical section and causing a race on variable x.

chapters.example: Two processes increment a shared counter initialized to 0. Each executes: read x; x = x + 1; write x. If they interleave, the final value may be 1 instead of 2.
chapters.trap: Writing the solution without guaranteeing progress; many students forget the bounded‑waiting condition.
chapters.leave: Hardware support for mutual exclusion is covered in the next chapter.

chapters.idea: Show Peterson’s algorithm and the role of hardware atomic instructions.
chapters.depth: Present the two‑process algorithm using turn and flag variables. Explain why the algorithm satisfies mutual exclusion, progress and bounded waiting. Describe test‑and‑set and compare‑and‑swap as hardware primitives that can replace the software solution. Some syllabi refer to this as "Synchronization Hardware".

figure.title: Peterson’s steps
figure.aria: Flowchart of Peterson’s two‑process mutual exclusion algorithm.

chapters.example: Two threads T0 and T1 use flag[2] and turn to enter a critical section that updates a shared balance of ₹10,000. Show the values of flag and turn before and after each step.
chapters.trap: Confusing i and j indices; many write the wait condition backwards.
chapters.leave: Hardware atomic instructions are detailed in the next chapter.

chapters.idea: Introduce mutex locks and counting semaphores as general synchronization tools.
chapters.depth: Define lock acquire and release operations. Explain binary semaphore as a lock and counting semaphore for resource pools. Show P (wait) and V (signal) operations with atomicity. Mention that some syllabi list these under "Mutex" and "Semaphores‑Deadlock".

figure.title: Semaphore value over time
figure.aria: Array showing how a counting semaphore decreases with each acquire and increases with each release.

chapters.example: Three processes request a pool of two identical printers. The semaphore is initialized to 2. Show the semaphore value after each P and V operation and which process proceeds.
chapters.trap: Forgetting to call V after using the resource; exam questions often omit the release step.
chapters.leave: Higher‑level abstraction of monitors is covered next.

chapters.idea: Explain monitors with condition variables for structured synchronization.
chapters.depth: Define monitor as a module that encapsulates shared data, procedures, a lock, and condition variables. Show wait, signal, and broadcast semantics. Clarify that only one process can be inside the monitor at a time. Some syllabi call this "Monitors" or "Classic Problems of Synchronization".

figure.title: Monitor entry/exit
figure.aria: Flowchart of a monitor procedure showing lock acquisition, optional wait, critical work, signal and lock release.

chapters.example: A bounded buffer of size 5. Producer calls put(item); consumer calls get(). Show the values of the buffer count, and when producers wait because the buffer is full and consumers wait because it is empty.
chapters.trap: Assuming signal wakes the same process that called wait; in monitors the waking process runs after the lock is released.
chapters.leave: Deadlock concepts are introduced in the next chapter.

chapters.idea: Model deadlocks and list the four necessary conditions.
chapters.depth: Present the system model with processes, resources, and allocation matrices. Define mutual exclusion, hold‑and‑wait, no‑preemption, and circular‑wait. Explain that all four must hold for a deadlock. Some syllabi refer to this as "Deadlock System Model".

figure.aria: Resource‑allocation graph showing a circular‑wait between two processes and two resources.

chapters.example: Two transactions T_A and T_B need locks on rows X and Y of a database. T_A holds lock X and requests Y; T_B holds Y and requests X. Show the graph and state that all four conditions are present.
chapters.trap: Missing the no‑preemption condition; many students think preemption alone can break a deadlock.

chapters.idea: Describe prevention strategies that break one of the necessary conditions.
chapters.depth: Explain each of the four strategies: (1) eliminate mutual exclusion for sharable resources, (2) require all resources before execution, (3) allow preemption of resources, (4) impose a total ordering on resource types. Mention that some syllabi list these under "Methods for Handling Deadlocks – Prevention".

figure.title: Prevention checklist
figure.aria: Block diagram showing four prevention methods leading to a safe system state.

chapters.example: A printing service requires all three printers at once. Show how requiring all three before starting avoids hold‑and‑wait, and compute the maximum number of concurrent jobs.
chapters.trap: Assuming that eliminating one condition guarantees deadlock‑free execution for all workloads; the chosen condition must be applied correctly.
chapters.leave: Avoidance, a more flexible technique, is introduced next.

chapters.idea: Present deadlock avoidance and the banker’s safety algorithm (advanced).
chapters.depth: Define safe and unsafe states. Show the need for future‑request knowledge. Explain the banker’s algorithm: check request ≤ need, pretend to allocate, run safety test, then commit. Only a few universities teach this in depth, so keep the explanation concise.

figure.aria: Decision tree of the banker’s algorithm showing the safety test path.

chapters.example: Three processes P0, P1, P2 and two resource types A (3 units) and B (2 units). Allocation matrix, max demand matrix, and an incoming request (P1 asks for (1,0)). Show step‑by‑step whether the request is granted.
chapters.trap: Skipping the safety test after a pretend allocation; many students grant the request directly.
chapters.leave: Detection and recovery are covered in the final chapter.

chapters.idea: Explain deadlock detection algorithms and recovery actions.
chapters.depth: Describe the resource‑allocation‑graph cycle detection for single‑instance resources and the Banker's‑like detection for multiple instances. Outline recovery methods: process termination, resource preemption, and rollback. Some syllabi list these under "Deadlock Detection and Recovery".

figure.aria: Directed graph showing a cycle that the detection algorithm must find.

chapters.example: Four processes compete for three identical printers. Show the allocation matrix, detect a cycle, and choose to abort the lowest‑priority process to break the deadlock.
chapters.trap: Assuming that killing any process always resolves the deadlock; the chosen process must release all its resources.
